questions.stem: What is the main feature of a sole trader business structure?

options.text: The business must have at least two owners
One person owns and runs the business
The business is owned by shareholders
A board of directors makes all decisions

questions.explanation: A sole trader is a business owned and operated by one person. It is the simplest business structure — no partners, no shareholders, no board.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 33–37 on sole traders and partnerships

questions.stem: A sole trader has limited liability, meaning their personal assets are protected if the business fails.
questions.explanation: A sole trader has UNLIMITED liability. This means the owner's personal assets (house, car, savings) can be used to pay business debts. This is a key risk of the sole trader structure.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 33–37 on sole traders and partnerships

options.text: A business run by the government
A business owned by two or more people who share responsibility
A large company listed on the stock exchange
A business that only sells to other businesses

questions.explanation: A partnership is a business structure where two or more people share ownership, responsibilities, profits and liabilities.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 33–37 on sole traders and partnerships

questions.stem: What does 'limited liability' mean for a company?

options.text: The company cannot make a loss
Owners can only lose the money they invested in the business
The company has a limit on how much it can earn
The owner must pay all debts personally

questions.explanation: Limited liability means the owners (shareholders) are only responsible for the amount they invested. Their personal assets are separate from the business debts.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 37–41 on limited liability and companies

questions.stem: Match each business structure to its key feature.

pairs.right: Two or more owners share profits

questions.explanation: Each business structure has different ownership, liability and decision-making characteristics. Choosing the right one depends on the specific needs and risks of the business.

questions.stem: The best business structure is always a company because it offers limited liability.
questions.explanation: There is no single 'best' structure. A company offers limited liability but is more expensive to set up and has more legal requirements. A sole trader is simpler and cheaper but carries more personal risk. The best choice depends on the specific business.

questions.stem: Which of these is a legal requirement for starting a business in Australia?

options.text: Hiring at least five employees
Registering a business name if trading under a name other than your own
Having a university degree in business
Owning a physical shop

questions.explanation: In Australia, if you trade under a name other than your own legal name, you must register that business name with ASIC. Other requirements may include an ABN, permits, or licences depending on the type of business.
questions.textbookRef: See pages 42–47 on legal requirements for starting a business

options.text: Australian Business Name — the trading name of a company
Australian Business Number — a unique 11-digit identifier for a business
Annual Business Notice — a tax report filed each year
Approved Business Network — a government support programme

questions.explanation: An ABN (Australian Business Number) is an 11-digit number that identifies your business to the government and community. Most businesses need one to operate legally in Australia.

questions.stem: Saying 'I chose sole trader because it is simple' is a strong justification linked to the business.
questions.explanation: A strong justification links the structure choice to specific features of THIS business — its risks, costs, number of owners, or growth plans. 'It is simple' is a generic textbook reason, not connected to the student's particular business.

questions.stem: Which factor is MOST relevant when choosing between a sole trader and a partnership?

options.text: The colour of the business logo
Whether you need to share decision-making and financial responsibility
What time the business opens
The name of the business

questions.explanation: The key factors in choosing a business structure include: how many owners there are, who makes decisions, how profits are shared, and who is liable for debts. These are the factors that should drive the choice.
